newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU sets summit date for talks on future.
newsitem.headline: EU sets summit date for talks on future.

text.p: The European Union agreed on Sunday to hold a special summit at the beginning of next month to jump-start talks on a new EU treaty that many in the bloc believe have become bogged down.
Britain, which opposes many of the proposals under consideration at the talks, immediately questioned the need for the meeting.

Ireland, the current EU president, said at an informal foreign minister meeting that the summit would be held in Dublin on October 5, somewhat earlier than originally planned but the only date acceptable in all 15 capitals.
The summit was ordered up by EU leaders at their last meeting, in Florence in June, as a response to fears that the talks, the so-called inter-governmental conference (IGC), were getting nowhere.
Designed to prepare the bloc for an influx of new members from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean, IGC talks have so far amounted to little more than a recital of wishes from individual countries.
"We have to get out of the very slow forward movement -- and that is being diplomatic," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, however, said he was not persuaded that having a meeting would serve much purpose at this stage.

"We have always held slightly more of the view that we have too many summit meetings," he said. "I am quite happy to be persuaded...but I start off with just a twinge of uncertainty as to whether this meeting will prove to have been entirely necessary."

The ruling British Conservative Party is sharply divided over the European Union and has been vehemently opposed to any move by the IGC that would dilute individual countries' sovereignty in favour of communal action.
The Dublin summit will be held three days before the Conservative Party's annual conference begins.

Others at the Tralee meeting said the summit was necessary if the IGC was to agree a new treaty by the middle of next year as planned. A draft treaty is to be presented to EU leaders at a second Dublin summit in December.
"This (summit) in October is to give political impetus," European Commission President Jacques Santer said.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said he would meet Kinkel, his German counterpart, on October 2 to draft a joint Franco-German position ahead of the summit.
Europe expected France and Germany to take the lead, he said.
Kinkel, meanwhile, accepted that Britain would pose a problem for the rest as the IGC progressed.
"Everybody will have to make an effort and with the British we will have to have a special talk," he told reporters.
